title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
relevance_reason: Audit of non-shared layer skipping, early exit and self-speculative decoding on standard Qwen2.5 models; no block is iterated in depth.
one_sentence: Three-seed audit of two online-search layer-skipping methods (ConfLayers, SWIFT) and two trained routers on Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B; separating search overhead from inference cost reverses the wall-clock ranking, and trained routing gives smaller measured speedups than layer counts imply.
key_contributions: Matched-seed, matched-task, matched-scale comparison restricted to methods with the same decision granularity (per-token, re-searched every 25-30 steps).
Frozen-replay decomposition of wall-clock into pure inference and online-search overhead, which inverts the naive speed ranking in three of four cells.
Supplemental measurement of LayerRoute and LayerDrop with verified genuine gating, a genuine full-model baseline and genuine compute skipping.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: no pretraining; LayerRoute/LayerDrop trained with a fixed LoRA budget
setup.baselines: vanilla autoregressive decoding; ConfLayers; SWIFT; LayerRoute; LayerDrop
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K (exact match), CNN/DailyMail (ROUGE-L), 100 held-out samples per task, 3 seeds

claims.claim: Among periodic-step methods, SWIFT has the best accuracy in three of four task/scale cells and ConfLayers is dominated everywhere, worst on GSM8K at 1.5B.
claims.regime: same backbone, same 100 samples, same 3 seeds; not FLOP-matched
claims.evidence_quote: SWIFT is the strongest method on accuracy in three of four cells; ConfLayers is dominated everywhere, with particularly large deficits on GSM8K at 1.5B.

claims.claim: Folding online-search time into wall-clock latency inverts the speed ranking: SWIFT's pure inference is 5-21% faster than ConfLayers's in all cells although its total wall-clock is slower in three of four.
claims.regime: measured wall-clock, batch size 1, single GPU
claims.evidence_quote: once decomposed, SWIFT's pure inference cost is faster than ConfLayers's in all four cells (5-21%), reversing the naive ranking in three of them.

claims.claim: Trained routers give real but modest measured speedups that are smaller than the savings implied by the number of skipped layers, attributed to per-layer router overhead.
claims.regime: measured wall-clock vs genuine full-model baseline; skip-rate proxy not reported numerically
claims.evidence_quote: both methods show modest but real speedups (1.08–1.33×) over a genuine full-model baseline, smaller than layer-count-implied theoretical savings would suggest; we attribute this to LayerRoute's router computation

claims.claim: Per-sequence trained gating collapses on multi-step reasoning at 1.5B.
claims.evidence_quote: LayerRoute's accuracy on GSM8K at 1.5B is essentially zero (0.003 mean, 1 of 300 samples correct)

claims.claim: All latency numbers are batch-size-1 single-GPU measurements with explicit synchronization and no warm-up.
claims.evidence_quote: All latency measurements use batch size 1 on a single GPU, with explicit device synchronization before and after each timed call

numbers.what: GSM8K exact match at 1.5B: ConfLayers vs vanilla
numbers.quote: particularly large deficits on GSM8K at 1.5B (0.077 vs. vanilla's 0.413)

numbers.what: Online-search overhead share of total cost: ConfLayers vs SWIFT
numbers.quote: ConfLayers's search overhead is small and stable (1.2–2.2% of total cost, near-zero variance across seeds); SWIFT's is larger (8.7–18.6% mean) and more variable (up to 28.7% on individual GSM8K/0.5B seeds)

numbers.what: GSM8K/1.5B per-query latency (ms): pure inference ConfLayers, SWIFT; overhead; ConfLayers wall-clock
numbers.quote: GSM8K/1.5B ConfLayers SWIFT 12366 9913 1.3% 12.4% 12485.4

numbers.what: LayerDrop measured speedup over full model
numbers.quote: LayerDrop, having no such per-query overhead, shows a somewhat larger, more consistent speedup (1.25–1.30×) despite lower average accuracy.

numbers.what: Evaluation size per task
numbers.quote: We evaluate 100 held-out samples per task, with an identical shuffle/seed recipe across dataset aliases

limitations: Two small instruction-tuned models, two tasks, 100 samples per task, 3 seeds, no power analysis, no warm-up, batch size 1 only; memory and quantization out of scope. Latency of vanilla decoding is not reported for the periodic-step methods, so their speedup over vanilla is not measured. Skip rates are not reported, so the proxy-vs-measured gap for trained routing is qualitative. LayerRoute is the author's own method and its original skip-rate claim was withdrawn.
survey_notes: Sections: adaptive depth (proxies vs clocks), systems (measurement protocol), neighbors (adaptive depth without sharing). What is matched: backbone, seeds (2024, 42, 123), tasks, scales and decision granularity; LayerDrop is matched to LayerRoute's LoRA training budget. Not matched: FLOPs or a common accuracy-latency frontier. Statement 1 (measured vs naive cost): how online overhead is accounted can invert method rankings, "once decomposed, SWIFT's pure inference cost is faster than ConfLayers's in all four cells (5-21%), reversing the naive ranking in three of them." Statement 2 (measured vs proxy): trained layer routing delivers "modest but real speedups (1.08–1.33×) over a genuine full-model baseline, smaller than layer-count-implied theoretical savings would suggest", attributed to router overhead at every layer. This is the non-shared analogue of the looped-model gap in tab:proxy_clock (Think-at-Hard, CHASE, per-token convergence). Caveats a survey author must state: no skip-rate numbers, so the size of the proxy gap is not quantified; no vanilla latency for ConfLayers/SWIFT; SWIFT is described as lossless by construction yet its GSM8K accuracy at 0.5B (0.303) differs from vanilla (0.180), which the paper does not explain; single-author audit with AI-assisted harness. Agrees with 2609.29867 that nominal compute is a poor proxy for latency.

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
relevance_reason: Early-exit ladder over unique (non-shared) TCN stacks for speech enhancement; no block is iterated in depth.
one_sentence: Per-frame early exit for causal speech enhancement compared against recipe-matched, compute-matched static models and measured int8 latency on an STM32N6; after repairing non-monotone exits, routing lies on the same quality-latency frontier as retrained statics.
key_contributions: Per-frame monotonicity regularizer with heads-only fine-tuning so deeper exits are never worse than shallower ones.
Shows most apparent routing headroom comes from frames where deeper exits hurt, and that repairing them removes the advantage over a compute-matched static frontier.
Measured int8 latency on a microcontroller NPU: analytic MACs mis-price graphs by 1.7x per MMAC and can mis-order models; dispatch overhead of dynamic execution is 2.2%.

setup.model_sizes: Conv-FSENet variants spanning 5.7-41.8 MMAC/s (widths H in {32,64,96,256}, stacks R in {1,2,3}, B=128)
setup.baselines: twelve static models trained from scratch with the same recipe; repaired static exits; routed models
setup.benchmarks: PESQ and SI-SDR on 824 test clips; measured ms/frame on STM32N6570-DK

claims.claim: Once fixed-depth models are compared fairly, per-frame routing adds little: the extracted static models form a competitive frontier, also under measured latency.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (realized MMAC/s) and measured latency; same data and training recipe
claims.evidence_quote: once the fixeddepth models are compared fairly, routing brings little advantage: indeed, the extracted static models form a competitive quality–compute frontier, which holds when considering measured latency instead of theoretical MACs.

claims.claim: Within one fixed ladder, early exit does cut measured on-device latency with little quality loss.
claims.evidence_quote: At H=256, routing reduces latency from 2.472 to 1.668,ms/frame while retaining 2.773 versus 2.781 PESQ.

claims.claim: Analytic MACs do not predict accelerator latency: time per MMAC varies 1.7x across topologies and MAC count can invert the latency ordering.
claims.evidence_quote: MAC count can even give the wrong ordering: (H=96, R=1) uses 21 % more MACs than (H=32, R=2) but runs 15 % faster.

claims.claim: Without the repair, deeper exits are worse than shallower ones on nearly half of the frames (overthinking), and this is where routing's apparent benefit comes from.
claims.evidence_quote: The apparent routing opportunity largely come from frames where deeper exits degrade the result, and the monotonicity repair removes much of that signal.

claims.claim: Common offline evaluation of routed models (gated sum) is optimistic because it updates the state of skipped stacks; deployed skipping keeps stale state.
claims.evidence_quote: This is far more realistic than common offline evaluation protocols, which compute the routed output as a gated sum, thereby effectively updating each exit even when unused.

numbers.what: Gain of repaired static family over scratch-trained statics
numbers.value: up to +0.11 PESQ; best PESQ at 30% less compute
numbers.quote: we achieve up to 0.11 higher PESQ for equivalent compute, and match the best PESQ at 30 % less compute.

numbers.what: Latency per analytic MMAC across ten topologies
numbers.quote: across ten measured topologies, execution time per analytic MMAC varies by 1.7×, from 82 to 137, µs/MMAC.

numbers.what: Two models with identical MACs and parameters, measured latency
numbers.quote: (H=32, R=2) and (H=64, R=1) have the same MACs and parameter count, yet take 1.00 and 0.75,ms per frame, respectively.

numbers.what: Routed H=32 vs static H=64,R=1 (PESQ, ms/frame)
numbers.quote: routed H=32 gives 2.639 PESQ at 0.769,ms/frame, while static H=64, R=1 reaches 2.684 at 0.751,ms

numbers.what: Policy cost and graph-splitting overhead
numbers.quote: Running the policy on the companion Cortex-M55 takes only 26 µs per frame, while splitting the enhancer into separate NPU graphs adds 2.2 % latency overhead.

numbers.what: Routed vs repaired-static frontier gap at matched compute
numbers.quote: at matched compute, their PESQ differs by less than 0.01 over the common range.

numbers.what: Compute saved on a difficult utterance by bypassing silence
numbers.quote: 74 % of speech-inactive frames take the bypass, versus 12 % of speech frames, reducing compute by 58.7 % over the warmed repeats relative to always running the deepest exit.

limitations: Speech-dense VoiceBank-DEMAND only; workloads with long pauses are untested. Small causal convolutional models, one device. Repaired best-PESQ match comes with a 1.0 dB SI-SDR drop.
survey_notes: Sections: adaptive depth (proxies vs clocks), systems, open problems (reporting standard). What is matched: realized average compute (MMAC/s), training recipe (same objective, optimizer, early stopping), data, and measured int8 latency on the same board; parameters are not matched (one ladder vs separate statics). Measured savings differ from proxy savings: nominal MACs mis-order latency, "(H=96, R=1) uses 21 % more MACs than (H=32, R=2) but runs 15 % faster", and per-MMAC latency spans 1.7x because each extra stack is another accelerator launch (depth is costly, width is cheap). Statement 1: against compute-matched, recipe-matched statics, dynamic depth "does not create a better latency-quality frontier"; quote used: "once the fixeddepth models are compared fairly, routing brings little advantage". Statement 2: the apparent benefit of adaptive depth can come from repairing overthinking rather than from saving compute, "The apparent routing opportunity largely come from frames where deeper exits degrade the result". Relevance to looped models: the same three confounds apply to loop-count policies (baseline must be a retrained fixed-loop model at matched realized compute, savings must be measured on the target hardware, and offline gated-sum evaluation overstates quality because skipped iterations still update state, analogous to missing KV for exited tokens). Nuance for tab:proxy_clock takeaway: here measured within-ladder latency gains exist at batch 1 without batching support, because depth is chosen per frame and dispatch costs 2.2%. Agrees with 2608.28846 on proxy vs measured cost.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
relevance_reason: Layer-pruning analysis of standard open-weight LLMs; motivates depth reuse but no block is iterated.
one_sentence: Similarity-guided removal of contiguous deep layer blocks plus QLoRA healing leaves QA benchmarks (MMLU, BoolQ) nearly intact until 20-55% of layers are removed, while C4 loss and reasoning tasks (GSM8K, HellaSwag) degrade with any pruning.
key_contributions: Angular-distance criterion to pick the block of n layers to prune, plus QLoRA healing on a single 40GB A100.
Family-specific collapse points for QA accuracy (Llama-2 45-55%, Mistral 35%, Phi-2 25%, Qwen 20%) and smooth loss degradation.
Evidence that deep layers matter for reasoning (GSM8K, HellaSwag) but less for knowledge QA.

setup.model_sizes: Llama-2 family up to 70B, Qwen family, Mistral-7B, Phi-2 (2.7B)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: QLoRA healing on a small amount of data (C4)
setup.baselines: unpruned models; simple heuristic dropping the deepest block excluding the final layer
setup.benchmarks: MMLU, BoolQ, C4 validation loss, CoT-MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag

claims.claim: Up to about half of the layers can be removed with minimal QA degradation for some open-weight models.
claims.evidence_quote: we find minimal degradation of performance until after a large fraction (up to half) of the layers are removed for some common open-weight models.

claims.claim: The pruning fraction at which QA accuracy collapses to random depends strongly on the model family.
claims.evidence_quote: a sharp transition to random accuracy at a pruning fraction around 45%-55% for models in the Llama-2 family, 35% for Mistral 7B, 25% for Phi-2, and 20% for models from the Qwen family.

claims.claim: Reasoning tasks are not robust: GSM8K and HellaSwag degrade with any amount of pruning, tracking the loss increase.
claims.evidence_quote: both GSM8K and HellaSwag, our two reasoning tasks, exhibit immediate degradation in performance with any amount of pruning, correlating with a similar decrease in the perplexity evals

claims.claim: Next-token loss on C4 degrades smoothly in proportion to the pruned fraction even where QA is flat.
claims.evidence_quote: if we look at the loss on next-token predictions for an IID dataset (C4 validation set), we find that the model is smoothly damaged in proportion to the fraction of the number of layers pruned.

claims.claim: Deeper layers are more similar to their neighbors than shallow layers, except the final layer, so dropping the deepest block (excluding the last layer) nearly matches the similarity-informed choice after healing.
claims.evidence_quote: after healing the damage with a small amount of QLoRA finetuning, we can achieve performance that nearly matches the more involved similarity-informed layer pruning strategy.

numbers.what: Fraction of Llama-2-70B layers removable before QA collapse
numbers.quote: for Llama-2-70B (Touvron et al., 2023) we can eliminate up to roughly half of the layers before the performance collapses.

numbers.what: Compute used per experiment
numbers.quote: such that each of our experiments can be performed on a single 40GB A100 GPU.

numbers.what: Healed loss behavior up to 80% pruning
numbers.value: slow growth up to at least 80%
numbers.quote: continuity and very slow growth in the healed loss (light blue) up to at least to 80% pruning fraction.

limitations: QA robustness does not extend to reasoning or loss; Qwen family behaves unusually; healing uses small QLoRA budgets; no latency measurements.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
survey_notes: Sections: neighbors (how standard Transformers use depth), lineage (motivation for reuse), open problems. Statement 1: in standard LLMs, knowledge QA survives removal of a large fraction of deep layers, "a sharp transition to random accuracy at a pruning fraction around 45%-55% for models in the Llama-2 family, 35% for Mistral 7B, 25% for Phi-2, and 20% for models from the Qwen family." Statement 2 (the caveat the survey must carry): reasoning does not survive, "both GSM8K and HellaSwag, our two reasoning tasks, exhibit immediate degradation in performance with any amount of pruning". Correction for 13_neighbors: if the survey cites deep-layer redundancy as motivation for looping, it must say the redundancy is task-specific (knowledge QA) and that deep layers are needed for reasoning; this is consistent with 2505.13898 (second-half layers refine the current prediction) and does not show that deep layers are useless. The residual intuition (representations change slowly with depth) is the same property that makes repeated application of one block plausible, but the paper does not test weight sharing. Contested cause: the paper offers two explanations (pretraining underuses deep layers, or shallow layers store knowledge), alongside pre-norm variance growth (2502.05795).

title: Megrez2 Technical Report
relevance_reason: Shares MoE expert pools across groups of three consecutive layers while attention and routers stay unique; component sharing, not an iterated block.
one_sentence: Device-oriented MoE LM that reuses one expert pool across each group of three adjacent layers (per-layer routers and attention kept) with pre-gated routing; Megrez2-Preview has 3B activated and 7.5B stored parameters, trained on 5T tokens.
key_contributions: Cross-layer expert sharing: unique parameters drop by roughly the group size while activated parameters stay unchanged.
Pre-gated routing combined with sharing so experts already loaded for a group need not be reloaded.
Megrez2-Preview release (31 layers, 64 experts per group, top-6, 4 shared experts per layer) with SFT and RLVR.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 5T tokens in three stages (1.5T, about 3T, more than 600B long-context)
setup.baselines: Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Qwen3-4B/8B, Phi-4-mini, Gemma-3-4B, GPT-4o-mini (public checkpoints)
setup.benchmarks: C-EVAL, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, MATH-500, GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP

claims.claim: Sharing each expert's parameters across n consecutive layers lowers total parameters by roughly n while activated parameters are unchanged.
claims.evidence_quote: cross-layer expert sharing reduces the number of unique parameters by roughly a factor of n while keeping the activated parameters unchanged.

claims.claim: Megrez2-Preview uses groups of three layers sharing a 64-expert pool after one dense first layer.
claims.evidence_quote: The model consists of 31 layers in total, with the first layer being a dense layer. Every three layers form a group that shares the expert parameters of the MoE module, which includes 64 experts per group.

claims.claim: Megrez2-Preview is reported competitive with or better than larger public models; the comparison is against public checkpoints trained on different data.
claims.evidence_quote: With only 3B activated and 7.5B stored parameters, Megrez2-Preview demonstrates competitive or superior performance compared to larger models on a wide range of tasks

claims.claim: Within a sharing group, an expert already selected does not have to be reloaded, which is the systems motivation for combining sharing with pre-gating.
claims.evidence_quote: within a group whose layers share a common expert pool, an expert that has already been selected need not be re-loaded, allowing the cache size and replacement policy to be tuned to the available hardware.

numbers.what: Pretraining tokens
numbers.quote: which is pre-trained on a diverse dataset containing 5 trillion tokens from multiple domains.

numbers.what: Megrez2 MATH-500 and GSM8K (EM), followed by Qwen2.5-3B
numbers.quote: Math Tasks MATH-500 GSM8K 81.6 83.6 65.9 86.7

numbers.what: Megrez2 C-EVAL and MMLU-Pro
numbers.quote: General Tasks C-EVAL MMLU-Pro 91.7 67.6 68.2 43.7

limitations: No ablation of shared vs unshared experts, no measured latency or memory despite the device-deployment motivation; all comparisons are to public checkpoints with different data.
survey_notes: Sections: lineage and design space (component-level cross-layer sharing), systems. Statement 1: cross-layer sharing has reached production MoE LMs in a partial form: "cross-layer expert sharing reduces the number of unique parameters by roughly a factor of n while keeping the activated parameters unchanged", with n=3 in Megrez2-Preview ("Every three layers form a group that shares the expert parameters of the MoE module"). Statement 2: the evidence is unmatched; the only performance claim compares to public checkpoints ("competitive or superior performance compared to larger models") and there is no shared-vs-unshared ablation or measured latency, so it cannot be cited as evidence that sharing preserves quality. Place it with MoEUT-style and FFN-sharing designs (e.g. One Wide FFN, 2309.01826) rather than with looped models: layers are distinct (own attention, own router), only the expert pool is reused, and nothing is iterated.

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
relevance_reason: Applies one shared Transformer block repeatedly over consecutive layers (with small per-layer transforms and unshared LayerNorm) in ViTs.
one_sentence: Weight multiplexing for ViTs: share MSA/MLP weights across consecutive blocks, add small unshared per-layer transformations and LayerNorms, and distill from a larger teacher; strict sharing alone destabilizes training and loses accuracy.
key_contributions: Diagnosis that strictly identical weights (including LayerNorm) cause large, fluctuating gradient norms and training collapse in weight-shared ViTs.
Per-layer linear transformations on attention and a depthwise conv in the MLP to diversify shared weights at small parameter cost.
Attention-level and hidden-state distillation from large teachers, yielding compact DeiT/Swin variants with equal depth.

setup.model_sizes: Mini-DeiT-Ti/S/B (3M-44M), Mini-Swin-T/S/B (12M-47M); Mini-DeiT-B with one layer of parameters is 9M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K, 300 epochs; teachers Swin-B (ImageNet-22k pretrained, 88M) and RegNet-16GF
setup.loops_train: 2 consecutive layers share weights (all layers per stage for Swin-T; all layers for the 9M DeiT-B)
setup.baselines: original DeiT and Swin; plain weight sharing; ablations of transformation and distillation
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-1K top-1, IN-Real, IN-V2, CIFAR, Flowers, Cars, Pets, COCO detection

claims.claim: Naive cross-layer weight sharing in ViTs makes training unstable and can collapse it as more layers are shared.
claims.evidence_quote: weight sharing across transformer layers makes the training become unstable, and even causes training collapse as the number of shared layers increases

claims.claim: At equal depth and data, plain sharing halves parameters but costs about 2 points of top-1 accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: After applying the weight-sharing method, the numbers of parameters of both models are halved, whereas the accuracy also decreases by 2% (#1 vs. #2, #6 vs. #7).

claims.claim: LayerNorm must not be shared across reused blocks because features at different depths have different statistics.
claims.evidence_quote: the layer normalization [5] in different transformer blocks should not be identical during parameter sharing, because the features of different layers have various scales and statistics.

claims.claim: With transformations plus distillation from a larger teacher, a model with half the layer parameters exceeds the original; this headline gain is confounded by distillation from an ImageNet-22k teacher.
claims.evidence_quote: with the proposed weight multiplexing, the Mini-Swin-B model with 12-layer parameters obtains 0.8% higher accuracy than the 24-layer Swin-B.

claims.claim: Extreme sharing (one layer of parameters) loses 2 points but cuts DeiT-B parameters 9.7x.
claims.evidence_quote: MiniDeiT-B with 9M parameters achieves 79.8% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, being 9.7 times smaller than DeiT-B (with 86 parameters and 81.8% accuracy).

numbers.what: Swin-S accuracy drop with plain sharing (4x fewer parameters)
numbers.quote: it leads to a 5.6% degradation in accuracy for Swin-S, although weight sharing can reduce the number of model parameters by fourfold.

numbers.what: Swin-T: params (M), MACs (B), ImageNet top-1
Mini-Swin-T: params (M), MACs (B), ImageNet top-1
Teacher used for Swin compression
numbers.quote: For compressing Swin [36], we adopt the ImageNet22k [16] pre-trained Swin-B with 88M parameters as the teacher model.

numbers.what: Swin-B size reduction and accuracy change
numbers.quote: it can reduce the size of the pre-trained Swin-B transformer by 48%, while achieving an increase of 1.0% in Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

limitations: Weight transformations slightly increase compute relative to plain sharing; accuracy degrades moderately as compression ratio increases. Compute (MACs) is not reduced, only parameters.
survey_notes: Sections: lineage (parameter sharing in Transformers), design space (relaxed sharing, per-iteration normalization), training (stability), beyond language. Statement 1: strict tying at equal depth hurts in vision Transformers, "After applying the weight-sharing method, the numbers of parameters of both models are halved, whereas the accuracy also decreases by 2%", and can collapse training. Statement 2: per-layer unshared LayerNorm and small per-layer transforms fix it, the vision precursor of relaxed recursive Transformers (2410.20672, layer-wise LoRA) and of per-iteration norms in looped LMs: "the layer normalization [5] in different transformer blocks should not be identical during parameter sharing". Regime caution: the headline that Mini models beat originals (e.g. "Mini-Swin-B model with 12-layer parameters obtains 0.8% higher accuracy than the 24-layer Swin-B") is confounded by distillation from a larger ImageNet-22k teacher; the clean iso-depth, iso-data comparison is Table 1 (-2 points). MACs are unchanged (Mini-Swin-T 4.6B vs Swin-T 4.5B), so this is a parameter-compression result, not a compute result. Supports the survey's 'untied beats tied at equal depth for generic perception' reading in 12_beyond_language.

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
relevance_reason: Replaces DiT's middle layers with one weight-tied, timestep-conditioned fixed-point block with input injection, iterated a variable number of times.
one_sentence: DiT with one pre layer, one implicit fixed-point layer (input injection, timestep-conditioned) and one post layer; 87% fewer parameters and 60% less training memory, better FID than DiT at low sampling compute but worse at high compute.
key_contributions: Prelude-core-coda denoiser whose core is solved by fixed-point iteration, allowing computation to be spread across more timesteps at fixed total cost.
Stochastic Jacobian-Free Backpropagation: random n no-grad iterations then m grad iterations; the 1-step gradient fails at ImageNet scale.
Reallocation heuristics (more iterations late in denoising) and fixed-point reuse across timesteps.

setup.model_sizes: 85-86M FPDM vs 674M DiT-XL/2 (28 layers); each block 24M parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet (class-conditional), FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Church at 256px; 8 V100, 4 days for ImageNet
setup.loops_train: n ~ U[0,N] no-grad plus m ~ U[1,M] grad iterations, M = N = 12
setup.loops_test: 1 to 68 iterations per timestep at fixed total block budget
setup.baselines: DiT-XL/2 trained for the same time on the same hardware
setup.benchmarks: FID-50K (DDPM and DDIM samplers) at 140/280/560 transformer-block forward passes

claims.claim: FPDM has 87% fewer parameters and 60% less training memory than DiT and better image quality when sampling compute or time is limited.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (total transformer-block forward passes) and matched training time
claims.evidence_quote: Compared to the state-of-the-art DiT model, FPDM contains 87% fewer parameters, consumes 60% less memory during training, and improves image generation quality in situations where sampling computation or time is limited.

claims.claim: The advantage disappears and reverses at larger sampling budgets.
claims.evidence_quote: At 560 forward passes, our method outperforms DiT with DDPM but not DDIM, and for more than 560 it is outperformed by DiT.

claims.claim: At matched per-timestep depth (26 iterations equal DiT's 28 layers) FPDM is slightly worse; its gains come from spreading the same compute over more timesteps.
claims.evidence_quote: Although our model is slightly worse than DiT at 26 iterations, it significantly outperforms DiT when smoothed across more timesteps, demonstrating the effectiveness of timestep smoothing.

claims.claim: The 1-step (Jacobian-free) gradient common in DEQs fails to optimize at ImageNet scale; multi-step and stochastic multi-step truncated unrolling work.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that 1-step gradient, the most common method for training DEQ [5] models, struggles to optimize models on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, whereas a multi-step version of it performs well

claims.claim: Allocating more fixed-point iterations to later denoising steps beats constant or decreasing allocation.
claims.evidence_quote: the increasing heuristic outperforms the contant and decreasing ones; allocating resources more toward the later stages of the denoising process improves generation quality and detail.

numbers.what: ImageNet FID at 140 block passes, DDPM/DDIM: DiT vs FPDM; params; training memory
ImageNet FID at 560 block passes, DDPM/DDIM: DiT vs FPDM
FID by gradient method with N=6: 1-step JFB, multi-step JFB, stochastic JFB
numbers.quote: 6 JFB (1-Step Grad) Multi-Step JFB Stochastic JFB 567.6 48.2 43.2

numbers.what: Best iterations per timestep at 280 block passes
numbers.quote: with 280 transformer block forward passes, we see that the optimal range lies between 4 and 8 iterations per timestep.

numbers.what: Training budget matching
numbers.quote: For a fair comparison, we train our models and baseline DiT models for the same amount of time using the same computational resources.

limitations: Gains are limited to low sampling budgets; at more than 560 block passes DiT is better. Some evaluations use 1000 images. Parameter count stated as both 85M and 86M.
survey_notes: Sections: beyond language (diffusion), design space (prelude-core-coda with input injection and timestep conditioning appears in vision in 2024), training (gradient horizon), adaptive depth (compute reallocation across timesteps). Statement 1 (regime): a weight-tied core beats an 8x larger untied DiT only at low inference budgets, "At 560 forward passes, our method outperforms DiT with DDPM but not DDIM, and for more than 560 it is outperformed by DiT", and is "slightly worse than DiT at 26 iterations" when per-step depth is matched. Statement 2 (training): "1-step gradient, the most common method for training DEQ [5] models, struggles to optimize models on the large-scale ImageNet dataset" (FID 567.6 vs 43.2 for stochastic multi-step), which parallels the recursive-reasoning finding that HRM's one-step gradient underperforms backpropagating through the last recursion (2510.04871) and argues against one-step gradients at scale. Agreement: more compute late in denoising is best here and in expert-choice diffusion LMs (2604.01622, low-mask-ratio steps). Training was matched by GPU time (8 V100, 4 days), not counted FLOPs.

title: Deep Equilibrium Optical Flow Estimation
relevance_reason: Solves the weight-tied RAFT/GMA update operator to a fixed point instead of unrolling a fixed number of recurrent steps.
one_sentence: Replaces RAFT-style unrolled recurrent flow refinement with a deep equilibrium solve (implicit or inexact gradients, sparse fixed-point correction, fixed-point reuse across frames), giving 4-6x less training memory, faster inference and better zero-shot KITTI/Sintel accuracy.
key_contributions: DEQ flow estimators applicable to RAFT and GMA update operators with O(1) training memory.
Sparse fixed-point correction loss that stabilizes DEQ training better than Jacobian regularization.
Fixed-point reuse across adjacent video frames to warm-start the solver.

setup.model_sizes: DEQ-RAFT-B 5.3M, DEQ-GMA-B 5.9M (same as RAFT/GMA), DEQ-RAFT-L 8.4M, DEQ-RAFT-H 12.8M
setup.loops_train: black-box solver to fixed point; RAFT uses L = 12 unrolled steps
setup.loops_test: Anderson solver stopping at relative residual 1e-3 with reuse; RAFT 32 steps
setup.baselines: RAFT, GMA (recurrent unrolled counterparts of identical structure and size)

claims.claim: DEQ flow estimators train with 4-6x less memory than their unrolled recurrent counterparts and allow faster inference via reuse and inexact gradients.
claims.evidence_quote: The use of these DEQ flow estimators allows us to compute the flow faster using, e.g., fixed-point reuse and inexact gradients, consumes 4 ∼ 6× less training memory than the recurrent counterpart

claims.claim: Unrolled RAFT refinement does not converge: activations oscillate after about 15 iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: while RAFT's iterative unrolling aims to mimic the iterative convergence, we find its activations usually oscillate at a relatively high level after about 15 update iterations.

claims.claim: Measured inference is about 20% faster than RAFT of the same structure and size (convergence stopping plus reuse vs 32 fixed steps).
claims.regime: iso_param, measured on one Quadro RTX 8000
claims.evidence_quote: it is in practice about 20% faster than the RAFT models with the same structure and size (blue bars).

claims.evidence_quote: our proposed fixed-point correction significantly outperforms the standard IFT training protocol by about 9%, and reduces the fixed-point error by a conspicuous margin, e.g., over 60%.

numbers.what: Zero-shot KITTI-15 improvement
numbers.quote: with an astonishing 21.0% error reduction in the F1-all measure and 14.9% improvement in EPE for KITTI-15 (while still using a similar training budget to RAFT [1]).

numbers.what: Model sizes
numbers.quote: The models are of exactly the same size as RAFT (5.3M) [1] and GMA (5.9M) [3] except they use DEQ flow formulation instead of recurrent updates.

numbers.quote: Together with the inexact 1-step gradient, the total training time can be streamlined over 45% compared with the IFT training schedule

numbers.what: Flow-estimation training memory reduction
numbers.quote: we observe that the memory cost of the flow estimation process reduces by a factor of over 4× (red bars).

survey_notes: Sections: beyond language (vision), adaptive depth (convergence stopping, warm start), training (inexact gradients, sparse deep supervision), mechanisms (oscillation vs convergence). Statement 1: an unrolled weight-tied refiner need not settle, "we find its activations usually oscillate at a relatively high level after about 15 update iterations", which parallels the survey's mechanisms discussion of looped LMs that lack a fixed point beyond the training depth. Statement 2: convergence-based stopping with warm starts gives measured, not proxy, savings in vision, "about 20% faster than the RAFT models with the same structure and size" and "a factor of about 1.6×" from fixed-point reuse; warm-starting a loop state from a neighboring position is untested in looped LMs (open problem). The sparse correction loss is a sparse form of the deep supervision used by recursive reasoning models and also uses the 1-step gradient successfully at 5.3M parameters, contrast with FPDM (2401.08741) where the 1-step gradient fails at ImageNet scale.

key_contributions: Joint multivariate fixed-point formulation of the DDIM chain that replaces serial sampling with a parallel solve.
Model inversion with O(1)-memory implicit or 1-step gradients through the chain.
Extension to stochastic DDIM/DDPM by treating sampled noise as input injection.

Statement 2: gains vanish when the chain is short ("the number of fixed point solver iterations needed for convergence becomes comparable to the length of diffusion chain"), so parallel loop solving should help most for many loops, which few looped LMs use. title: Block Diffusion: Interpolating Between Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: Diffusion LM that is autoregressive over blocks and diffuses within blocks; iteration is over denoising steps, not depth.
one_sentence: Block diffusion LMs generate blocks autoregressively with KV caching and denoise tokens within each block; with variance-reducing noise schedules they set a new diffusion perplexity state of the art and support arbitrary-length generation.
key_contributions: Block-autoregressive diffusion with KV caching and parallel within-block sampling.
Shows that the remaining gap to AR at block size 1 is due to gradient variance, and proposes data-driven noise schedules.
Efficient vectorized training keeping cost below 2x diffusion training.

title: Expert-Choice Routing Enables Adaptive Computation in Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: MoE routing and timestep-dependent capacity in diffusion LMs; adaptive compute without depth recurrence.
one_sentence: Expert-choice routing fits non-causal diffusion LMs: deterministic load balance doubles wall-clock training speed over token-choice, and giving more expert capacity to low-mask-ratio denoising steps lowers perplexity at matched FLOPs up to 8B-A1B.
key_contributions: EC vs TC routing for DLM MoE with measured throughput and wall-clock convergence.
Timestep-dependent expert capacity schedules compared at matched expected FLOPs, with a learning-efficiency explanation.
Retrofit of a pretrained TC DLM (LLaDA-MoE) to EC by swapping the router and fine-tuning.

survey_notes: Sections: adaptive depth (expert-choice as compute allocation), systems (measured vs proxy throughput), neighbors (diffusion LMs). Statement 1 (systems): fixed per-expert capacity removes stragglers and gives measured gains, "EC achieves 52.1 TFLOP/s/GPU, 1.5–2.1× higher than all TC variants" and "1.3–1.5× faster decoding"; the paper flags that TC throughput "uses the theoretical per-expert FLOPs", a proxy-vs-measured distinction. Mixture-of-Recursions (2507.10524) uses expert-choice routing for per-token recursion depth, so this supports expecting real, not only nominal, savings from capacity-bounded depth routing. Statement 2 (adaptive compute across refinement steps): "Linear-reverse consistently achieves the lowest perplexity under matched FLOPs", i.e. late (low-mask) denoising steps deserve more compute; this agrees with FPDM's increasing heuristic (2401.08741). Regime: iso_param and iso_data for EC vs TC, matched expected FLOPs for schedules; 8B-A1B results are single runs.

title: Masked diffusion LLMs can use EoS tokens for hidden reasoning
relevance_reason: Shows hidden computation in padding positions of masked diffusion LLMs; no depth recurrence.
one_sentence: Longer generation windows padded with EoS tokens improve LLaDA1.5 and Dream-v0 on addition, entity tracking, Sudoku, GSM8K and two-hop tasks, and patching EoS hidden states shifts answers, showing EoS positions carry hidden computation.
key_contributions: Controlled prompting experiments separating generation length, decoding steps and appended EoS tokens.
Causal activation patching of EoS hidden states between generations.
Contrast between fully bidirectional models and block-causal LLaDA2.0-mini, which does not benefit.

setup.baselines: same models with shorter generation length or fewer EoS tokens; Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 for reference
setup.benchmarks: Addition, Entity Tracking, Sudoku, GSM8K, two-hop reasoning

claims.claim: Adding EoS tokens improves masked diffusion LLM performance in a controlled prompting experiment.
claims.evidence_quote: In a controlled prompting experiment, we confirm that adding EoS tokens improves the LLMs' performance.

claims.claim: Transferring EoS hidden states between generations raises the likelihood of the counterfactual answer, so EoS states are causally used.
claims.evidence_quote: we perform a causal intervention and transfer the hidden states of the EoS tokens between generations, which increases the models' relative likelihood of outputting the counterfactual answer.

claims.claim: Longer generation windows raise accuracy up to saturation, the largest gain being LLaDA1.5 on entity tracking.
claims.evidence_quote: Across models, LLaDA1.5 on E NTITY T RACKING has the greatest improvement from 23% to 67% from generation length 20 to 80.

claims.claim: Block-causal LLaDA2.0-mini does not benefit from trailing EoS tokens and breaks with many of them.
claims.evidence_quote: This is contrasted by LLaDA2.0, which almost does not benefit from trailing EoS tokens. When appending 64 or 128 EoS tokens, its generation even breaks, and it outputs only EoS tokens.

numbers.what: Sudoku gain from 128 appended EoS tokens
numbers.quote: Until 128 EoS tokens, Dream improves by 3% and LLaDA1.5 by 10%.

limitations: Three models only; no circuit-level decoding of what EoS states compute; broad definition of reasoning; MoE model excluded from patching.
survey_notes: Sections: safety (hidden computation, opaque serial depth), neighbors (diffusion LMs), theory (padding as extra compute). Statement 1 (safety): extra non-content positions give masked diffusion LLMs a hidden computation channel with causal evidence, "transfer the hidden states of the EoS tokens between generations, which increases the models' relative likelihood of outputting the counterfactual answer"; this belongs in tab:safety_map's adjacent-evidence column next to 2606.20560 (opaque serial depth of diffusion LMs). Statement 2: the effect depends on attention pattern, absent in block-causal LLaDA2.0 ("almost does not benefit from trailing EoS tokens"), and it matches the theoretical picture of masked diffusion models as padded looped Transformers (2510.13117), where padding supplies width for computation. Not looped in depth; inference-time manipulations of off-the-shelf models, so no comparison regime applies.
